1.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֞ע הַ⁠כְּנַעֲנִ֤י מֶֽלֶךְ־עֲרָד֙ יֹשֵׁ֣ב הַ⁠נֶּ֔גֶב כִּ֚י בָּ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל דֶּ֖רֶךְ הָ⁠אֲתָרִ֑ים
1.note: The event narrated in 21:1–3 may have happened before or after Aaron died, which was narrated in 20:23–29. The Hebrew word translated as “and” at the beginning of this verse does not necessarily mean that this event happened after the previous event. If it would be helpful in your language, you could introduce this event in a way that does not indicate whether it came before or after the previous event. Alternate translation: [Now it also happened that the Canaanite, the king of Arad, the one dwelling in the Negev, heard that Israel had come the way of the Atharim]

Here the author is introducing **the Canaanite, the king of Arad, the one dwelling in the Negev** as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [the Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the Negev]

Here, the word **Atharim** could be: (1) a proper name for a city. In this case, the road probably led to Atharim. Alternate translation: [the road to Atharim] (2) a word that means “spies.” In this case, this is probably the road that the Israelite men traveled on when they explored the land (see Numbers 13–14). Alternate translation: [the way the Israelite spies had traveled]

The pronoun **him** refers to the nation of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and he fought against Israel, and he took captive from Israel a captive]
This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

2.note: The term **said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root: **vowed a vow**. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [solemnly vowed]

The Israelites are repeating forms of the verb **give** in order to intensify their expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [If you give, give]
Here, **hand** represents the control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into my power]

The pronoun **my** refers to the people of Israel, who speak of themselves here as a single person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [into the hands of our people]

2.q: אִם נָתֹ֨ן תִּתֵּ֜ן אֶת הָ⁠עָ֤ם הַ⁠זֶּה֙ בְּ⁠יָדִ֔⁠י וְ⁠הַֽחֲרַמְתִּ֖י אֶת עָרֵי⁠הֶֽם
2.note: Israel is presenting a possible condition, that they will devote the cities of the Canaanites to destruction if Yahweh gives this people into their hand. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Suppose you give this people into my hand. In that case, I will devote their cities to destruction]

3.note: Here, **voice** represents what the people of Israel said. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh listened to what Israel said]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he gave the Canaanite into their hand]

The pronoun **he** refers to the people of Israel, even though Yahweh was the subject earlier in the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and they devoted them and their cities to destruction. And they called]
The word **Hormah** is the name of a place.

4.note: The author is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites set out]

The author is using **the soul of the people was short** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the people became impatient.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the people became impatient]

4.q: וַ⁠יִּסְע֞וּ מֵ⁠הֹ֤ר הָ⁠הָר֙ דֶּ֣רֶךְ יַם־ס֔וּף לִ⁠סְבֹ֖ב אֶת־אֶ֣רֶץ אֱד֑וֹם
4.note: Here, **to** marks **go around the land of Edom** as the goal or purpose of **they set out from Mount Hor by the way of the Sea of Reeds**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

5.note: The term **spoke** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

The people are using the question form to complain against God and Moses. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You brought us up from Egypt only to die in the wilderness!]
The pronoun **you** refers to God and Moses together. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Why have you two brought us up]
Here, **to** marks **die in the wilderness** as the goal or purpose of **brought us up from Egypt**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.
Here, **soul** represents the appetite of the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and we loathe]

6.note: Here, the phrase **fiery ones** identifies what kind of serpents these were. Most likely, they were called “fiery” because of how their venom affected people, probably making people swell and have fevers. If your readers would not be familiar with what a fiery serpent is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the venomous serpents]
The pronoun **they** refers to the serpents. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the serpents bit the people]

7.note: The term **said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

7.q: וַ⁠יָּבֹא֩ הָ⁠עָ֨ם אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֜ה וַ⁠יֹּאמְר֣וּ חָטָ֗אנוּ כִּֽי־דִבַּ֤רְנוּ בַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ וָ⁠בָ֔⁠ךְ
7.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And the people came to Moses and said, “We have sinned because we spoke against Yahweh and against you.]
The pronoun **him** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and let Yahweh remove]

The people are using **the serpent** to represent all of the serpents that Yahweh had sent among them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the serpents]

8.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [a fiery serpent]

Yahweh is presenting a possible condition, that anyone who has been bitten will live if he looks at the image on the banner. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [that whoever is bitten will live if he looks at it]

The expression **all the bitten ones** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [everyone whom a serpent has bitten]

9.note: The pronoun **it** refers to the bronze serpent that Moses made. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and he put the bronze serpent on the banner]

9.q: אִם נָשַׁ֤ךְ הַ⁠נָּחָשׁ֙ אֶת אִ֔ישׁ וְ⁠הִבִּ֛יט אֶל נְחַ֥שׁ הַ⁠נְּחֹ֖שֶׁת וָ⁠חָֽי
9.note: The author is presenting a possible condition, that a man who had been bitten would live if he looked at the bronze serpent. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [a man who had been bitten by a serpent and looked at the bronze serpent would live]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [anyone]

10.note: The author is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

11.note: The author is using **upon the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “opposite” or “facing.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [{is} across from Moab]

The author is using **from the rising of the sun** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to the east.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on the east side]

13.q: כִּ֤י אַרְנוֹן֙ גְּב֣וּל מוֹאָ֔ב בֵּ֥ין מוֹאָ֖ב וּ⁠בֵ֥ין הָ⁠אֱמֹרִֽי
13.note: Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

14.q: עַל כֵּן֙ יֵֽאָמַ֔ר בְּ⁠סֵ֖פֶר מִלְחֲמֹ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה
14.note: The phrase **it is said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

The expression **it is said** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people say]

The **Book of the Wars of Yahweh** is the name of an ancient written record. If your readers would not be familiar with what this is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [in the ancient written account called the Wars of Yahweh]

The author is using the possessive form to describe the **Wars** as ones characterized by belonging to **Yahweh**, that is, wars that Yahweh fought. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wars that Yahweh fought]

14.q: עַל כֵּן֙ יֵֽאָמַ֔ר בְּ⁠סֵ֖פֶר מִלְחֲמֹ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה
14.note: The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [As a result, it is said in the Book of the Wars of Yahweh]

14.q: אֶת וָהֵ֣ב בְּ⁠סוּפָ֔ה וְ⁠אֶת הַ⁠נְּחָלִ֖ים אַרְנֽוֹן
14.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [There is Waheb in Suphah, and there are the wadis of Arnon]

15.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and there is the slope of the wadis]

15.q: וְ⁠אֶ֨שֶׁד֙ הַ⁠נְּחָלִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר נָטָ֖ה לְ⁠שֶׁ֣בֶת עָ֑ר וְ⁠נִשְׁעַ֖ן לִ⁠גְב֥וּל מוֹאָֽב
15.note: The author is speaking of **the slope of the wadis** as if it were a living thing that could stretch out and lean against something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [goes as far as the seat of Ar … and is at the border of Moab]

16.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And from there they went to Beer]

16.q: הִ֣וא הַ⁠בְּאֵ֗ר אֲשֶׁ֨ר אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ לְ⁠מֹשֶׁ֔ה
16.note: Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

16.q: אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ לְ⁠מֹשֶׁ֔ה אֱסֹף֙ אֶת הָ⁠עָ֔ם וְ⁠אֶתְּנָ֥ה לָ⁠הֶ֖ם מָֽיִם
16.note: The term **said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

17.q: אָ֚ז יָשִׁ֣יר יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶת הַ⁠שִּׁירָ֖ה הַ⁠זֹּ֑את
17.note: The author is using the word translated as **Then** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

17.q: אָ֚ז יָשִׁ֣יר יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶת הַ⁠שִּׁירָ֖ה הַ⁠זֹּ֑את
17.note: The term **sang** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

The Israelites are speaking to the **well**, which they know cannot hear them. They are doing this to communicate to the people listening to them that they feel very strongly about the well. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if they were speaking directly to the people about the well. Alternate translation: [May water flow up from the well]

18.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [the princes and nobles of the people dug it]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And from the wilderness they traveled to Mattanah]

18.q: בְּאֵ֞ר חֲפָר֣וּ⁠הָ שָׂרִ֗ים כָּר֨וּ⁠הָ֙ נְדִיבֵ֣י הָ⁠עָ֔ם בִּ⁠מְחֹקֵ֖ק בְּ⁠מִשְׁעֲנֹתָ֑⁠ם
18.note: Here, the poet could mean that: (1) the **princes** and **nobles** authorized the digging of the well using their scepters and **staffs**. In this case, they do not dig the well themselves. Alternate translation: [A well, princes authorized its excavation, the nobles of the people authorized its construction; they authorized it with a scepter, with their staffs] (2) the **princes** and **nobles** dig at least part of the well themselves, using **scepter** and **staffs**. Alternate translation: [A well, princes excavated it themselves, the nobles of the people dug it themselves, using a scepter, using their staffs]

19.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and from Mattanah they traveled to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel they traveled to Bamoth]

20.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and from Bamoth they traveled to the valley]

The author is speaking of the top of the Pisgah as if it were a living thing that could have a **head**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the top of the Pisgah]

Here, **the face of** represents the surface of the wasteland that could be seen from the mountain peak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the surface of the wasteland]
Here, the word translated as **wasteland** could be: (1) a description of the area. Alternate translation: [the deserted area] (2) a name. Alternate translation: [Jeshimon]

21.note: The author is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated **saying** in [1:1](ta:01).

22.note: The pronoun **me** refers to the people of Israel, even though it is singular and the following pronoun **We** is plural. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Let us pass over in your land. We will not turn aside]

Israel is using the possessive form to describe a **way** that is characterized by belonging to the **king**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [On the main road used by the king]

23.q: וְ⁠לֹא נָתַ֨ן סִיחֹ֣ן אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל֮ עֲבֹ֣ר בִּ⁠גְבֻל⁠וֹ֒
23.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And Sihon did not give Israel permission to pass over in his border]
The pronoun **he** refers to Sihon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Sihon came to Jahaz, and he fought against Israel]

24.note: The author is using the phrase **struck him to the mouth of the sword** as a common expression of the culture to mean “killed him and his army with swords.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Israel put him to the edge of the sword] or [And Israel killed him and his people with swords]

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

25.note: The author says **all the cities of the Amorite** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [in every city of the Amorite]

The author is using **its daughters** as a common expression of the culture to mean “its surrounding villages.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in all its nearby villages]

26.q: כִּ֣י חֶשְׁבּ֔וֹן עִ֗יר סִיחֹ֛ן מֶ֥לֶךְ הָ⁠אֱמֹרִ֖י הִ֑וא
26.note: Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

26.q: וְ⁠ה֣וּא נִלְחַ֗ם בְּ⁠מֶ֤לֶךְ מוֹאָב֙ הָֽ⁠רִאשׁ֔וֹן וַ⁠יִּקַּ֧ח אֶת כָּל אַרְצ֛⁠וֹ
26.note: Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

26.q: וְ⁠ה֣וּא נִלְחַ֗ם & וַ⁠יִּקַּ֧ח אֶת כָּל אַרְצ֛⁠וֹ מִ⁠יָּד֖⁠וֹ
26.note: The pronoun **his** refers to the former king of Moab, not to Sihon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and he had fought … and he had taken all the former king of Moab’s land from him]

Here, **hand** represents the control of the former king of Moab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from his control]

27.q: עַל כֵּ֛ן יֹאמְר֥וּ הַ⁠מֹּשְׁלִ֖ים בֹּ֣אוּ חֶשְׁבּ֑וֹן תִּבָּנֶ֥ה וְ⁠תִכּוֹנֵ֖ן עִ֥יר סִיחֽוֹן
27.note: The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [As a result, the ones speaking in parables say]
The term **say** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

The expression **be built and be established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let them build and establish it]

28.q: אֵשׁ֙ יָֽצְאָ֣ה מֵֽ⁠חֶשְׁבּ֔וֹן לֶהָבָ֖ה מִ⁠קִּרְיַ֣ת סִיחֹ֑ן
28.note: Here the poets are speaking as if Sihon’s conquering army were **a fire** and **a flame** that went out from Heshbon. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [an army went out from Heshbon, a destroying force from the city of Sihon]

Here the poets are speaking of the fire as if it were a living thing that could consume **Ar of Moab** the way a person eats food. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It destroyed Ar of Moab]

The phrase **the lords of** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. Alternate translation: [it swallowed the high places of Arnon]

29.q: אוֹי לְ⁠ךָ֣ מוֹאָ֔ב אָבַ֖דְתָּ עַם כְּמ֑וֹשׁ
29.note: The poets are speaking to Moab, which they know cannot hear them. They are doing this to communicate to the people listening to them that they feel very strongly about the destruction of Moab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if they were speaking directly to the people about Moab. Alternate translation: [How terrible it is for Moab! The people of Chemosh have perished!]

The poets are using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, dismay over the destruction that has come on Moab. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Terrible things have happened to you, Moab]

The poets are using the possessive form to describe a **people** who are characterized by their worship of **Chemosh**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [worshipers of Chemosh]

The word **Chemosh** is the name of the god whom the people of Moab worshiped. If your readers would not be familiar with who this is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [their god]
The pronoun **He** refers to Chemosh, the god of Moab. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Chemosh has given his sons as fugitives and his daughters]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as captives]

30.note: The pronoun **we** refers to the Amorites who composed and recited this song. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And we, the Amorites, shot them … And we, the Amorites, made desolate]

Here, the pronoun **we** could refer to: (1) the Amorites who were ruled by Sihon. In this case, the pronoun **them** refers to the Moabites whom they defeated. Alternate translation: [And we, the Amorites, shot them, the Moabites … And we made desolate] (2) the Israelites who defeated Sihon. In this case, the pronoun **them** refers to the Amorites who were ruled by Sihon, whom the Israelites defeated. Alternate translation: [And we Israelites shot those Amorites … And we made desolate]

The words **And we shot them. Heshbon has perished as far as Dibon** are a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. Alternate translation: [And their descendants perished, Heshbon as far as Dibon]

The phrase **which is** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. Alternate translation: [fire as far as Medeba]

32.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the Israelites whom Moses sent. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the Israelites captured its daughters]

The author is using **its daughters** as a common expression of the culture to mean “its surrounding villages.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [its nearby villages]

33.note: The author is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

Here the author is introducing **Og, the king of the Bashan** as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Now there was a king named Og who ruled the Bashan, and he went out]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **battle**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to wage war at Edrei]

34.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֤ה אֶל מֹשֶׁה֙ אַל תִּירָ֣א אֹת֔⁠וֹ כִּ֣י בְ⁠יָדְ⁠ךָ֞ נָתַ֧תִּי אֹת֛⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת כָּל עַמּ֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת אַרְצ֑⁠וֹ
34.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh said to Moses, “Do not fear him, because I have given him and all his people and his land into your hand.]
The term **said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

The words translated as **Do not fear** are an imperative, but they communicate a condition rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a condition for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a condition. Alternate translation: [Since you have no need to fear him]
If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Yahweh giving Og before the phrase **into your hand**. Alternate translation: [I have given him into your hand]
Here, **hand** represents the control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into your control]

35.q: וַ⁠יַּכּ֨וּ אֹת֤⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת בָּנָי⁠ו֙ וְ⁠אֶת כָּל עַמּ֔⁠וֹ
35.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the Israelites, while the pronoun **him** refers to Og. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites struck Og and his sons and all his people]

The author says **not a survivor remained for him** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [until no one was left alive]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [until not a survivor remained alive for him]
